hook.line: Tomás has been hearing opinions all week about whether Altamira will really buy the block, and now people ask what he thinks. Saying what you think is easy. Saying what you don't think changes the verb.
hook.es: No creo que Altamira quiera hablar con nosotros.
hook.en: I don't think Altamira wants to talk to us.

examples.en: I think you're right. (to a friend)
I don't think you're right. (to a friend)

examples.es: Creo que Vale está en la cocina.
examples.en: I think Vale is in the kitchen.

examples.es: No creo que Vale esté en la cocina.
examples.en: I don't think Vale is in the kitchen.

examples.es: No me parece que sea justo.

examples.en: Do you think Vale is coming today? (to a friend)

examples.es: No creo que Vale venga hoy.
examples.en: I don't think Vale is coming today.

rule:
Compare the pairs above. *Creo que tienes razón* puts a claim on the table, so the verb stays as it is: *tienes*, *está*, *es*.

*No creo que tengas razón* declines to put the claim on the table. Spanish marks that by switching the verb to the wish form: *tengas*, *esté*, *sea*, *venga*.

So the *no* in front of *creo* is the trigger. The same goes for *me parece*: *Me parece que es justo*, but *No me parece que sea justo*.

A question like *¿Crees que viene?* usually keeps the plain verb, because you are still just asking.

English never changes the verb here (I think it is, I don't think it is), so watch for the *no*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the subjunctive after a negated opinion verb. The plain form is the indicative.

readAndPick.es: No creo que Vale esté en la cocina.
options: I think Vale is in the kitchen.
I don't think Vale is in the kitchen.
I think Vale isn't in the kitchen.
I don't think you're right. (to a friend)
I think you're right. (to a friend)

readAndPick.es: No me parece que sea justo.
options: I think it's fair.
I don't think it's fair.
I think it was fair.

readAndPick.es: Creo que Altamira quiere comprar el barrio.
options: I don't think Altamira wants to buy the neighbourhood.
I think Altamira wants to buy the neighbourhood.
I think they're coming.
I don't think they're coming.
I don't think you all are coming.
I think Altamira is lying.
I don't think Altamira is lying.
It seems to me Altamira lied.

readAndPick.es: No creo que mi abuela lo sepa.
options: I think my grandmother knows it.
I don't think my grandmother knows it.

readAndPick.es: Creo que Mariana tiene la respuesta.
options: I don't think Mariana has the answer.
I think Mariana has the answer.

readAndPick.es: No creo que podamos abrir hoy.
options: I don't think we can open today.
I think we can open today.
I don't think they can open today.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *está* or *esté* and type the whole sentence: *No creo que Vale ___ en la cocina.*
yourTurn.answer: No creo que Vale esté en la cocina.
yourTurn.why: After *no creo que* the verb takes the wish form: *esté*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *tienes* or *tengas* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Creo que ___ razón.*
yourTurn.why: With no *no* in front, you are claiming it, so the plain verb: *tienes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I don't think it's fair.
accept: No me parece que sea justo.
yourTurn.why: The negative opinion calls for the wish form of *ser*: *sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I think Altamira wants to buy the neighbourhood.
yourTurn.answer: Creo que Altamira quiere comprar el barrio.
accept: Me parece que Altamira quiere comprar el barrio.
yourTurn.why: A plain opinion keeps the plain verb: *quiere*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Creo que Vale viene hoy.*
yourTurn.answer: No creo que Vale venga hoy.
accept: No me parece que Vale venga hoy.
yourTurn.why: Add *no* and the verb moves to the wish form: *venga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Me parece que es justo.*
yourTurn.answer: No me parece que sea justo.
yourTurn.why: *No me parece que* works like *no creo que*: *sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: I don't think you have the answer.
yourTurn.answer: No creo que tengas la respuesta.
accept: No creo que sepas la respuesta.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I don't think we can open today.
yourTurn.answer: No creo que podamos abrir hoy.
yourTurn.why: The wish form of *poder* for *we* is *podamos*.

pitfalls.wrong: No creo que es una buena idea.
pitfalls.right: No creo que sea una buena idea.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English keeps *is* after I don't think; Spanish switches to *sea*.
Almost. Without a *no* you are claiming it, so the verb stays plain: *es*.

pitfalls.wrong: No creo que Vale viene hoy.
pitfalls.right: No creo que Vale venga hoy.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *No creo que* always pulls the next verb into the wish form: *venga*.

pitfalls.wrong: Creo que no tengas la respuesta.
pitfalls.right: Creo que no tienes la respuesta.
pitfalls.why: Careful. A *no* after *que* does not trigger the switch; only a *no* in front of *creo* does, so here the verb stays plain: *tienes*.

personal: Say one thing you think about Bogotá with *creo que*, then one thing you don't think with *no creo que*. For example: *Creo que el café es bueno. No creo que el tráfico sea fácil.*
